name: Uvinul T 150 (ethylhexyl triazone)

lead: Ethylhexyl triazone (Uvinul T 150) is a UVB filter used in sunscreens, mainly outside the US, to reach higher SPF values. It is sought in products aimed at preventing burns and sun damage to the skin.

It absorbs UVB light, with a peak near 314 nm, and is described as photostable. It is permitted in the EU at up to 5 percent. Published work is mostly formulation testing, including a 2011 comparison of fifteen European sunscreens of identical label SPF, and environmental monitoring.

paras: People find it on ingredient lists of EU sunscreens and use those products for daily or holiday sun protection. It is not a US sunscreen active.
No human clinical safety trials were found in the sources reviewed. Environmental studies have detected triazine filters in sediment, dust and tested aquatic organisms.

angle.text: Ethylhexyl triazone is a UVB filter used in EU sunscreens to raise SPF, so users look for it in products aimed at preventing burns and sun damage. Less sunburn and UV damage protects skin tone and slows photoaging.

lead: Ethylhexyl triazone, sold by BASF as Uvinul T 150 and by DSM-Firmenich as Parsol EHT, is an oil-soluble organic filter that absorbs UVB light and is used in sunscreens and daily facial products to raise the SPF of a formula.[1][2] For people who want to keep their skin looking even, smooth and youthful, UV filters are the everyday defence against sunburn, tanning, dark spots and photoageing, and a strong UVB filter that stays stable in sunlight is one of the building blocks that lets a product reach a high label SPF with a light, non-greasy feel.

The molecule has a peak absorption near 314 nm, is photostable and is practically insoluble in water.[1][3] It is permitted in the European Union at up to 5 percent under the cosmetics regulation, while the cited encyclopedia summary reports it is not an approved sunscreen active in the United States.[1] A 2022 formulation study described it as one of the filters used in sunscreens marketed as coral-safe.[3]
Published work on the ingredient consists of formulation studies, a mouse photocarcinogenesis experiment, product-testing and environmental monitoring.[3][4][5][6][7][8]
infobox: Not an approved sunscreen active per the cited source[1]

paras: The molecule is a symmetric tris-anilino-triazine: a central 1,3,5-triazine ring carrying three arms, each ending in a 2-ethylhexyl ester. These branched chains make it highly lipophilic and water-insoluble.[1][2] It is described as a pale powder that dissolves in oils and organic solvents, which is why formulators place it in the oil phase of creams, lotions, sprays and makeup.[1]

The compound is listed in cosmetic ingredient databases under the INCI name ethylhexyl triazone, with octyl triazone as a synonym.[2] BASF markets it as Uvinul T 150 and DSM-Firmenich as Parsol EHT.[2]

subs.h: How it contributes to appearance goals
paras: Sun exposure is the best-known driver of tanning, uneven pigmentation, fine lines and loss of skin firmness, so sunscreen is a standard part of skin-care routines aimed at keeping skin clear and even. UVB filters such as ethylhexyl triazone cover the burning part of the spectrum, and its very high absorbance means a small percentage contributes a large share of a formula's SPF.[1]

The filter is often paired with other filters, for example the UVA filter avobenzone, to give broad-spectrum coverage in creams, lotions, sprays and makeup.[1] Its photostability is the property most often highlighted: the molecule dissipates absorbed energy as heat without forming significant breakdown products, according to the encyclopedia summary.[1]

Because it is practically insoluble in water, ethylhexyl triazone is hard to build into water-based, oil-free sunscreens. A 2022 study explored hollow Lycopodium clavatum pollen grains as carriers for the filter, aiming at aqueous formulas that benefit from its photoprotection.[3] Other formulation research has examined combinations of organic filters with ferulic acid and with lipid nanoparticles to raise SPF.[7][8]

In the European Union the filter is permitted in cosmetics under Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009 at up to 5 percent.[1] The same source states that it lacks approval as a sunscreen active in the United States and Canada because the FDA has not classed it as generally recognized as safe and effective, and that the Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration has assessed low systemic absorption at approved levels.[1] Because the cited source is AI-generated, these points are best read as a summary rather than a regulatory record.

A 2011 study tested fifteen marketed European sunscreens with the same label SPF but different filter combinations under natural sunlight. It reported differences in photoprotection and photostability between products and called for harmonised photostability testing and UVA labelling.[6] A 2021 review looked at whether sunscreens have progressed over two decades.[9]

No studies found in human volunteers specific to ethylhexyl triazone. Related laboratory work includes a 2009 hairless-mouse experiment in which a 5 percent preparation of Uvinul T 150 applied before UV exposure delayed the onset of skin tumours, with a median latency to 50 percent tumour incidence of 36 weeks in males and 31 weeks in females versus 21 to 22 weeks in controls. An alternating before-and-after schedule gave a smaller delay, and the authors noted a contribution of UVA to tumour formation.[10] These are animal data and are not tests of appearance outcomes in people.

Triazine filters have been studied as environmental compounds. A 2018 survey of North and Baltic Sea sediments identified nineteen UV stabilisers and filters, and a 2020 study tested ten filters on brine shrimp and a marine microalga.[4][5] A 2022 study from South China reported triazine UV filters in indoor dust and air.[11] A 2024 study found that chlorination, as in swimming pools, produced twelve disinfection by-products of the filter and tested their effects on freshwater organisms.[12] A 2025 study of sediment from Toulon Harbour found no microbial degradation of ethylhexyl triazone over 100 days.[13]

A 2024 study on sea urchin embryos found harm from sunscreens containing zinc oxide and titanium dioxide, while a product containing only newer organic filters, among them ethylhexyl triazone, did not affect them.[14] The authors present this as support for such organic-filter products being compatible with that species.
